course.title: Atomic – Cambridge Lower Secondary Mathematics — Stage 7

unit.title: Collecting Data
unit.blurb: Planning a statistical investigation: asking a question, choosing what data to collect, tally charts and frequency tables, and choosing a sample.
unit.subject: maths

O1.t: Plan an investigation, record data in tally charts and frequency tables, and recognise categorical, discrete and continuous data.

O2.t: Understand populations and samples, and choose a sample that represents the population.

p: 1. Ask a **question** you can answer with data. 2. **Collect** the data. 3. **Organise** it in a table or chart. 4. **Interpret** it and answer the question.
**Categorical** data are words (favourite colour). **Discrete** data are counted (number of pets). **Continuous** data are measured (height).
Make one mark for each result. Every fifth mark crosses the four before it: |||| , so you can count in fives.
The **frequency** is the total number of tallies.

lesson.t: Why the type of data matters
p: The type of data decides how you collect and show it. Categorical data (colours) cannot be put in number order, so a bar chart with gaps fits.
Continuous data (heights) can take any value, so you group it into classes such as 140 ≤ h < 150, with no gaps and no overlaps, so every value fits exactly one class.

lesson.t: A good question or a vague one?
lesson.q: Compare: 'Do students like sport?' and 'How many hours of sport do Stage 7 students do each week?'
steps: 'like' means different things, and the answer is only yes or no
it names the group and the quantity

p: The **population** is everyone you want to know about. A **sample** is a smaller group you ask.
A good sample is **big enough** and **represents** the whole population, for example by choosing people at **random**.

lesson.q: To find out what Stage 7 students think of lunch, Ravi asks his 5 best friends. Why is this a poor sample?

lesson.t: Why a random sample is fairer
p: If every member of the population has the same chance of being chosen, no group is left out on purpose, so the sample tends to look like the population.
A bigger sample gives results that change less from sample to sample, but it costs more time. Choose a size that is practical and big enough.
Asking only your friends, or only people in one place, can give biased results.
